summary: Extends IKEv2 so a VPN gateway can assign a remote client an IPv6 configuration, such as addresses and prefixes. The configuration payloads in RFC 4306 handle IPv4 well but make IPv6 awkward. It is Experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join a VPN, the server hands you an address to use. The old way fit the older style of address poorly, so this adds a better way to give out the new style.

questions: how to assign ipv6 addresses in ikev2
subtitle: Assigning IPv6 prefixes to VPN clients via IKEv2.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 configuration payloads (RFC 4306) assign IPv6 addresses to VPN clients in a way that mirrors IPv4, but IPv6's architecture expects link-local addresses, prefix-based addressing, and support for multiple prefixes. This makes it hard to use IPv6 features like DHCPv6, prefix sharing, and cryptographically generated addresses.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds two new IKEv2 configuration attributes: INTERNAL_IP6_LINK (negotiates a virtual link with link-local addresses) and INTERNAL_IP6_PREFIX (assigns whole prefixes instead of individual addresses). The gateway also sends a LINK_ID identifier for reauthentication and child SA creation.
tldr.outcome: VPN clients can now properly configure virtual IPv6 interfaces with all standard IPv6 features. The gateway ensures address stability across reauthentication and can share prefixes among clients for local area network use.

today: RFC 5739 is Experimental. While it defines a cleaner approach to IPv6 configuration in VPN scenarios, adoption has been slow. Most deployed VPN clients and gateways continue to use RFC 4306's simpler single-address model or have moved to DHCPv6 alternatives. The RFC remains valuable as a reference for IPv6-aware VPN design and is particularly relevant for scenarios that require multiple addresses or prefix sharing.

sections.title: The Limitations of IKEv2's IPv6 Configuration
sections.content:
RFC 4306 (IKEv2) includes a configuration mechanism for assigning IPv6 addresses to VPN clients, but it treats IPv6 addresses just like IPv4 addresses: the gateway picks a single address from a single prefix and sends it to the client. This approach ignores several key aspects of IPv6's design.

IPv6 specifies that every interface must have a link-local address (address prefix FE80::/10) for local network operations. It also enables technologies like DHCPv6, Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGAs), and prefix sharing. The old IKEv2 mechanism supported none of these. This RFC extends IKEv2 to assign complete IPv6 prefixes instead of individual addresses, enabling full IPv6 functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way was like saying 'here is your address, 2001:db8::1'. The new way says 'here is your whole street, 2001:db8::/64, so you can give out addresses to your friends if you want'.

sections.title: What the New Solution Enables
sections.content:
With prefix assignment, VPN clients can now host local area networks (WiFi, Bluetooth) without NAT, because each client receives a unique prefix block. A gateway can assign multiple prefixes to a single client for various purposes (site renumbering, multihoming, unique local addresses). The client can choose its own interface identifiers, which is essential for Cryptographically Generated Addresses and other identity-based techniques.

The solution also defines a virtual interface linking the client and gateway. Both sides choose their link-local interface identifiers during the initial IKEv2 exchange. The gateway sends a LINK_ID identifier that the client can use later for reauthentication or child SA creation, ensuring the client continues using the same prefixes and addresses across network changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Now the VPN can give you enough addresses to run a small network. You pick some of your interface identifiers, and the gateway remembers you when you come back, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: The IKEv2 Configuration Exchange
sections.content:
During the IKE_AUTH exchange, the client sends a new configuration request attribute INTERNAL_IP6_LINK, specifying the interface identifier it wants for the link-local address. The gateway responds with an INTERNAL_IP6_LINK attribute containing the gateway's link-local interface identifier and a LINK_ID (an opaque identifier for future reference), followed by one or more INTERNAL_IP6_PREFIX attributes, each specifying a prefix and its length (usually /64).

The client configures its link-local address as FE80::XXXX (where XXXX is the client's chosen interface identifier) and derives other unicast addresses from the assigned prefixes using any interface identifiers it chooses. The gateway commits to not assigning the same prefixes to other clients, so the client does not need to perform Duplicate Address Detection.
sections.plainLanguage: Client says 'I want interface ID 1234 for link-local'. Gateway replies 'OK, I'm 5678, here are your prefixes 2001:db8::/64 and 2001:db9::/64, remember ID abc123'. Client fills in the rest.

sections.title: Maintaining Addresses Across Reconnection
sections.content:
When a VPN client needs to reauthenticate (renew the IKE SA), it includes the LINK_ID it received earlier in its INTERNAL_IP6_LINK configuration request. The gateway verifies that this client is still authorized to use that link. If yes, the gateway returns the same link-local interface identifiers and (usually) the same prefixes, allowing the client to keep using the same IPv6 addresses.

This mechanism is crucial for address stability: a user can disconnect and reconnect to the same VPN gateway and immediately resume using the same IPv6 addresses, without the need to renumber or reconfigure applications.
sections.plainLanguage: When you come back, you say 'remember me, ID abc123?' The gateway checks and says 'yes, here are your same prefixes again', so your email and other services keep working.

sections.title: Identifying the Virtual Link
sections.content:
When creating child SAs (the actual security associations that protect traffic), either peer can include a LINK_ID notification containing the IKEv2 Link ID. This identifies that the child SA is related to the virtual IPv6 link and should use the prefixes configured during IKE_AUTH, rather than other Security Policy Database (SPD) entries the peers might have.

This avoids ambiguity when the same peers use IPsec for multiple purposes (e.g., one VPN connection for a client-gateway link and another for site-to-site connectivity). The LINK_ID notification appears in the CREATE_CHILD_SA request but not in child SA rekeys or IKE SA rekeys.
sections.plainLanguage: When setting up a secure tunnel for data, you attach a label saying 'this is for the virtual link, use the VPN prefixes', so the gateway knows which rules to apply.
